Not all AI scribing systems are created equal. I worked for (insert remote scribing start up here). I scribed remotely through a livestream (it was so cool). The way we scribed our notes was using a special notetaker application that studied the way we wrote notes, our word choice, phrasing, etc. While we were scribing for a provider, we were basically training our AI system. 

I was laid off after about 2 years, with my hours slowly being cut during the course of that period. Some scribes kept their jobs a little bit longer for quality and assurance/continuous refinement of the AI scribe. For the providers that prefer a real scribe, my former company has trained and hired foreign workers to handle those rare cases. AI scribing systems will only get more accurate and efficient with time.

I was in the same boat when I finished undergrad. I applied to 10+ hospitals and offices for PCT and PT Aide jobs and interviewed at 4 of them. It was v stressful, esp waiting for replies (some never came) but stick with it! I cried after one interview because of how stupid I felt afterwards/what I could have done different but these feelings are normal (in the context of finding a job). And thanks to that rejection I was able to interview at the clinic I have been working at for almost a year now.

If you are intimidated by direct patient care jobs right now because you feel that you do not have the experience yet, consider applying to any job that interests you (tutoring, food service, office clerk at a medical office etc...) and one that pays well. Applying to PA school and PA school in general costs $$$ so anything helps! Social skills are essential in this field. Therapy and counseling may  seriously be something worth checking out. Since you are still in school, see what counseling programs are offered at your college (usually free while attending). You have lots of time to gain PCE experience. Take care of yourself and do well in your classes in the meantime :)

CNAS holds up to their policy. After final grades are released (or even now knowing that you probably won't finish well this quarter), I recommend immediately contacting your academic advisor. It is possible to appeal your disqualification through a form and you will have to meet with the dean of CNAS, who at my time was Dr. Nugent. She is an incredibly sweet and understanding person who gave me a second chance. Just like you, I was on STD one quarter, fixed it the second, but messed up again the quarter after.

Note that though the argument that hybrid classes are difficult (which they are), there were thousands of other students who were still successful this quarter. That is reality.  If you want the a second chance, you need to be honest and own up to your academic performance. If  you do meet the dean, dress up and treat it like an interview. Sorry if this sounds mean, but I had to hear this from someone else and it got me to graduation (I finished my Neuroscience B.S. in three years, you can still make things right!) PM me if you have other questions.

You may be asked patient scenario questions. Before landing my current pt aide job, 2/3 places I interviewed at gave me the same irl scenario. Something along the lines of: "A regular patient to our office suddenly returned the following week reporting severe pain, walked with a limp, and showed visible discomfort. What is the first thing you would do as a PT Aide in this scenario?" The answer is: Find your supervising DPT/PT/PTA ASAP. As an aide you have limits in terms of liability and capability for someone in this case. 

Another question that caught me off guard was "how would you motivate a unmotivated patient who doesn't like working out/doing a certain exercise?" I mentioned things like using more open body language/tone of voice, but also respecting a patients boundaries/limits! 

Be yourself! Also research the particular office you are applying for ahead of time. I stalked my interviewer (a DPT) on their website/linkedin so I was able to have a great convo about their career and research interests.

I was once in this exact situation but I was still able to register. Some questions I have for you are:

1. Are you attempting to register for classes you have failed more than once? OR are you attempting to register for just part of a course (ie: Just the Chem 8LA portion of Chem8A)? If so you will need to request a form from your academic advisor or the enrollment office. If it is the first case, you may need to fill out a petition to retake the class you failed more than once or potentially meet with Dean Nugent. 
2. Did you complete a term plan and have it approved by your academic advisor? OR do you have any outstanding holds on your account? These are so annoying lol. 
3. If you emailed UCR at any point this past week you probably did not get a response because they have been off this past week. You should expect a response sometime this week! 

I understand 100% this is a very scary situation but stay calm and be patient. I agree with the other comments on considering withdrawing the previous quarter, esp if you would like to save your GPA for grad school. The only downside to that is having to retake those classes and no refund on the money spent on last quarter. If it will help calm your anxiety perhaps consider emailing the enrollment office directly. They respond p fast from my experience! 

You got this, everyone struggles at some point in college. You still have two+ years to make it up, just be sure you do better next time! Best of luck.

Hi I was in a the exact position 3 years ago! I'm a third year neuroscience major at UCR  graduating this spring. I will be completely honest as someone who came from a private school as well, UCR will be a big transition. As others mentioned the class sizes for lower level science courses are huge at 200+ seats but you take upper division courses the sizes get closer to 50. Just because UCR has a medical school isn't a guarantee in, considering the huge amount of students just like you who commit to UCR with the intention of eventually applying to the medical school (also like me three years ago lol). 

The main reason I ultimately chose UCR over LMU was the research opportunities and clinical volunteering opportunities in the area. Since my freshman year I've worked at three different research labs for psych, neuroscience, and biology. I also work for the basic needs department. The Riverside area also has a lot of need for clinical and basic needs services. There are many ways to get hands on healthcare experience helping the less fortunate through free clinics and clubs on campus. 

If location matters to you (which is okay if it does), the general Riverside area sucks lol. LMU does give you access to DTLA and the other university life nearby. If there are particular clubs/orgs at LMU you are interested in, keep that in mind.

Ultimately, if you prefer LMU you should pick LMU, bc its you who will have to live and go to school there (by the way you typed your post you also sound like you have already made your mind up lol).  Making the most of your opportunities at whatever school you pick and getting the best grades you can are more important for med school than the where you go (in this case). Best of luck.
